lead: The Chinese remainder theorem (CRT) says that one congruence modulo a product can be split into separate congruences modulo coprime factors. Solve the small pieces, then glue the answers back into one value modulo the product. It exists because many modular calculations are easier with small moduli. It is used to speed up RSA decryption, to share secrets, and to solve systems of congruences in coding and cryptography.
prereq: You need: congruences from Chapter 2.1 and modular inverses from Chapter 2.2.

blocks.text: Two integers m and n are coprime when gcd(m,n)=1. A list of moduli is pairwise coprime when every pair has gcd 1. For example, 3, 5 and 7 are pairwise coprime; 4 and 6 are not, because gcd(4,6)=2.

Let m₁, m₂, …, mₖ be pairwise coprime moduli, and let M = m₁m₂⋯mₖ. Let a₁, a₂, …, aₖ be any chosen residues. The system x ≡ a₁ (mod m₁), x ≡ a₂ (mod m₂), …, x ≡ aₖ (mod mₖ) has exactly one solution modulo M.
x ≡ a₁ (mod m₁), x ≡ a₂ (mod m₂), …, x ≡ aₖ (mod mₖ)
blocks.where: x is the unknown integer; aᵢ is the required residue for modulus mᵢ; the moduli mᵢ are pairwise coprime; M is their product; the solution is unique modulo M.

blocks.text: Uniqueness is simple. If x and x′ both solve the system, then mᵢ divides x − x′ for every i. Because the mᵢ are pairwise coprime, their product M also divides x − x′. So x ≡ x′ (mod M). The theorem does not say the solution is a small number; it says the solution is one class modulo M.

The generalized form drops the pairwise coprime condition in a limited way. For moduli that are not coprime, a system may have no solution or several solutions modulo the product. A solution exists only when every pair of congruences agrees on their common factor, that is, aᵢ ≡ aⱼ (mod gcd(mᵢ,mⱼ)). The full proof is not needed here. For cryptography, the coprime case is the one used.

sections.h3: The construction with Mᵢ and inverses

blocks.text: The standard construction turns each congruence into a term that is 1 modulo its own modulus and 0 modulo every other modulus. Set Mᵢ = M / mᵢ. Since the moduli are pairwise coprime, gcd(Mᵢ, mᵢ)=1, so Mᵢ has an inverse modulo mᵢ. Call that inverse yᵢ, so Mᵢ yᵢ ≡ 1 (mod mᵢ).

blocks.where: Mᵢ = M/mᵢ; yᵢ = Mᵢ⁻¹ mod mᵢ; the whole sum is reduced modulo M at the end.

items: For each i compute Mᵢ = M/mᵢ.
Find yᵢ = inverse of Mᵢ modulo mᵢ, using the extended Euclidean algorithm.

blocks.text: Why the terms work: for j ≠ i, Mⱼ contains the factor mᵢ, so Mⱼ ≡ 0 (mod mᵢ). The only term that survives modulo mᵢ is aᵢMᵢyᵢ, and Mᵢyᵢ ≡ 1 (mod mᵢ), so the sum is ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ).
This construction is a formula, not a search. It solves any number of pairwise coprime congruences in one pass. Always reduce the final sum modulo M. The unreduced sum can be much larger than M.

RSA decryption computes c^d mod n, with n = pq. CRT lets the receiver compute the result modulo p and modulo q separately, then combine. Each exponentiation uses numbers about half the bit length, so it is faster than one exponentiation modulo n. The private key often stores p, q and the CRT inverses for this reason. See Unit 4, Public Key Cryptography and Hashing, for RSA itself.

Secret sharing uses CRT as one classic construction. A dealer picks pairwise coprime moduli and gives each person one residue. A large enough set of residues determines the secret modulo the product; a smaller set leaves many possible values. This is a threshold idea, related to but different from Shamir's polynomial scheme.

CRT also appears in fast arithmetic: represent a big integer by its residues modulo several small primes, do addition and multiplication componentwise, then reconstruct. It is a bridge between one large modulus and several small ones.

figure.caption: Each congruence contributes one term aᵢ × Mᵢ × yᵢ, built so that it is right modulo its own number and 0 modulo the other two. The terms 140, 63 and 30 add to 233, which is 23 modulo 105.

spec.aria: Three columns for the moduli 3, 5 and 7, each working out M, its inverse y and its term (140, 63 and 30); arrows lead to a sum box giving 233 and then 23 modulo 105.

examples.question: Solve the system x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 5), x ≡ 2 (mod 7). Give the unique solution modulo the product and check it.
steps: The moduli are 3, 5 and 7. gcd(3,5)=1, gcd(3,7)=1 and gcd(5,7)=1, so they are pairwise coprime.
M₁ = 105/3 = 35. Modulo 3: 35 ≡ 2. The inverse of 2 modulo 3 is 2, because 2×2=4≡1 (mod 3). So y₁ = 2.
M₂ = 105/5 = 21. Modulo 5: 21 ≡ 1. The inverse of 1 modulo 5 is 1. So y₂ = 1.
M₃ = 105/7 = 15. Modulo 7: 15 ≡ 1. The inverse of 1 modulo 7 is 1. So y₃ = 1.
Reduce modulo M: 233 mod 105 = 23, since 105×2 = 210 and 233 − 210 = 23.
Check: 23 mod 3 = 2, 23 mod 5 = 3, 23 mod 7 = 2. All three match.
examples.answer: The unique solution modulo 105 is x ≡ 23 (mod 105).
examples.check:
m = [3, 5, 7]
a = [2, 3, 2]
M = 1
for mi in m:
    M *= mi
x = 0
for ai, mi in zip(a, m):
    Mi = M // mi
    yi = pow(Mi, -1, mi)
    x += ai * Mi * yi
x %= M
print(x)

traps: Using moduli that are not pairwise coprime. Check gcd(mᵢ,mⱼ)=1 for every pair before applying the formula.
Forgetting the final reduction modulo M. The sum 233 is not the usual answer; the solution is 23 modulo 105.
Using the inverse modulo the wrong number. yᵢ is the inverse of Mᵢ modulo mᵢ, not modulo M.
Thinking the solution must be less than every modulus. The unique class is modulo M, and its smallest non-negative representative can be larger than each mᵢ.

quiz.q: State the Chinese remainder theorem for pairwise coprime moduli.
quiz.a: If m₁, …, mₖ are pairwise coprime and M is their product, then the system x ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ) has exactly one solution modulo M.

quiz.q: Why does the term aᵢMᵢyᵢ equal aᵢ modulo mᵢ and 0 modulo every other mⱼ?
quiz.a: For j≠i, Mᵢ contains mⱼ, so Mᵢ≡0 (mod mⱼ). Modulo mᵢ, Mᵢyᵢ≡1, so aᵢMᵢyᵢ≡aᵢ (mod mᵢ).
M=20. M₁=5, y₁=1, term=5. M₂=4, y₂=4, term=32. S=37, x=17. Check: 17 mod 4=1, 17 mod 5=2.

quiz.q: A student applies CRT to x ≡ 1 (mod 4), x ≡ 2 (mod 6). Explain what goes wrong and whether a solution exists.
quiz.a: The moduli 4 and 6 are not coprime; gcd(4,6)=2. A solution needs 1≡2 (mod 2), which is false. So the system has no solution.

quiz.q: In RSA decryption with n=pq, why can CRT split the computation modulo p and q?
quiz.a: Because p and q are coprime and n is their product, CRT says c^d mod n is determined by c^d mod p and c^d mod q. Compute two smaller exponentiations and combine.

quiz.q: What is the modulus of uniqueness for a CRT solution with moduli m₁,…,mₖ?

beyond: Not for the exam. CRT extends to polynomials over a field, where it helps in coding theory and fast algorithms. It also appears in hardware arithmetic units and in some secret-sharing schemes. Search for Garner's algorithm to see a practical way to reconstruct a number from residues. Search for polynomial Chinese remainder theorem for the next step.
